utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-05-88-T, the versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. All the accused are here. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution present, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness doesn't need any protective measures, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we are ready for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you still intend to take three and a half hours, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I've tried to reduce my examination, Mr. President. I will try to keep it to three hours or -- or even less, if possible. I think I've already cut out a decent amount, including exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Which means that, if Mr. Thayer keeps to his estimate, one of you at least would be required to start his or her cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius. To my right I have Judge Kwon and Judge Stole. To my left, I have Judge Prost. Together we compose this Trial Chamber. You are about to start giving evidence. And before you do so, you're kindly requested to enter a solemn declaration required by our Rules that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I swear that I will state the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, General. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You first are going to be asked questions by Mr. Thayer, who will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Not all of them, but most of them. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name and spell it for the record.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm Cornelis Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, you were commissioned as an officer in the Dutch army in 1969 and retired with the rank of major-general?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In 1965, I entered the service. And I left the service as a general-major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when did you retire, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you served in Bosnia for approximately six months in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct. From the end of February 1995 until early September I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please tell the Trial Chamber how you came to serve with UNPROFOR in Bosnia. Was this a posting you sought out?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In this specific case, I did. That's not usual. Ordinarily you're appointed to a post. But previously I had been offered another position that was inconvenient for me for personal reasons, and when asked what I did want, I said that I wanted to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your position when you entered your service in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In Bosnia I served as Chief of Staff of what was originally called the Command for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BH Command. The name was later exchanged to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were your duties and responsibilities as Chief of Staff to the BH commander?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: A commander is supported in his duties by a staff, run by the Chief of Staff, who is responsible for day-to-day command of the operations, ensuring that the reports are ready on time, that the commander is properly informed, that the assignments are executed, and that plans are drafted and that the situation is kept track of, all daily routine duties by the staff are on its -- the aegis of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, General, who was the BH commander under whom you served as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: With the British Lieutenant General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. It was a French colonel, Philippe Coiffet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in addition to Colonel Coiffet, did you also have a military assistant, or an MA?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had a Dutch lieutenant-colonel with me, who basically assisted me in all my daily activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that lieutenant-colonel's name, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Andrew de Ruiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when General Smith was away, who stood in for him?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was the -- the senior-ranking general at that point. He would take over. And in most cases, that was Major-General Gobillard, the commander of the Sarajevo Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this time, sir, during your service, what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I was brigadier-general at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to ask you some questions now concerning your contacts with members of the VRS high command. Do you recall the names of any VRS Main Staff officers you heard of during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Regularly the man I had the most contact with was General Milovanovic. As far as I know, he was the Chief of Staff of General Mladic. He was also, I would say, the first designated contact for me. When he was absent, I would be passed to somebody else by the -- on the phone. Sometimes that was General Mladic himself, but I also spoke several times with General Tolimir and with General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any other VRS Main Staff officers whose name you heard or were aware of during the period of your service in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. And there was little point to speaking with generals -- excuse me, speaking with officers below the level of the general, because no decisions were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: What I mean is that if you had a question or a request, the only useful answers would be from somebody at the general's level. Apparently they were authorised to take decisions, and beneath that level at best the question would be accepted and passed on and you would have to wait for an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's spend a few moments and -- and discuss some of these Main Staff officers whom you listed. You referred to General Milovanovic. Do you recall meeting him in person at any time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. In the first week after my arrival, my predecessor introduced me to the contacts of the other parties there, and for the VRS that was General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you -- you stated a few moments ago that you had the most contacts with General Milovanovic. Was there any protocol regarding with whom you would be in contact on the VRS side that governed who you typically would have had contact with?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a protocol. There were agreements that staffs would have contact only with their own levels. So BH Command would deal with the army command. The commander of the sectors would interact with the army corps commanders of the troops that they were in contact with. Within the staff, ordinarily the Chief of Staff would speak with the Chief of Staff and the commander would speak with the commander. But, of course, there were occasional exceptions if somebody was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if General Milovanovic were away, for example, was there anyone in particular that would stand in for him that you recall, other than speaking with General Mladic or General -- General Tolimir on occasion, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. As far as I was concerned, it depended on the coincidence of who happened to be present at that point. If General Milovanovic was not present, I would speak with one of the aforementioned other generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And regarding what types of matters would you deal with General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, that would be a wide variety of matters. First of all, if there had been any acts of violence, such as shooting incidents, then that would be discussed or protest -- protest would be lodged. And there might also be discussions about permission to transfer a convoy to bring supplies to the civilians in the enclaves. We also discussed exchanging prisoners between the different parties. Other conversations addressed is prisoners of war. Excuse me. Casualties or injured. And what also happened quite regularly: If injured people had to be evacuated, then there would be negotiations about that as well, because authorisation was needed to transport across the territory of one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to General Gvero, when do you recall first having contact with him?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was on 11 July, the day that the Srebrenica enclave fell. And I believe I remember that the next day, on 12 July, I spoke with him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll talk about those conversations in a little while, sir. To your knowledge, where were these VRS high command officers, Mladic, Milovanovic, Tolimir, and Gvero? Where was this -- this Main Staff headquartered to your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I knew at the time, that was in Pale. Later on I learned that that was incorrect, but we always contacted people in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to meeting General Milovanovic. Where did you in fact meet him?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was also in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you met him in Pale, did you meet him in what you understood to be the VRS Main Staff headquarters, or were you in another building?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, it didn't look like a barracks or headquarters, but the building did look like it served an official purpose. And at any rate, there were some VRS servicemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that time, what was your understanding of physically where in -- in proximity did the actual Main Staff have its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was somewhere near Pale, but I didn't have an immediate interest in the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, have you ever heard of the facilities located in Han Pijesak or Crna Reka, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Later on -- and when I say later on, I mean after I had already returned from Bosnia, I understood that that's where the VRS headquarters were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you wanted to contact the VRS Main Staff by telephone, can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, how those phone calls, as far as you understood it, physically were made. Just step by step, please.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, making phone calls wasn't that difficult. We had a direct connection with a post in Pale that we could call to. And I had a female interpreter who would call and establish contact. And subsequently the conversation would take place, but if we wanted to send written messages, there was a UNMO post in Pale and we had a fax connection with that and could send the -- a fax to the UNMOs, who would subsequently bring that message to the VRS authorities present at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you referred to a female interpreter a moment ago. Do you recall her name?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Her first name was Svetlana. Unfortunately, I don't remember her surname any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of any other interpreters upon whose services you regularly relied?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I thought there was one called Zdravko, but I don't remember that exactly because in 90 per cent of all cases, I worked with Svetlana..

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by whom was she actually employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: She had served many of my predecessors. I think by the time I entered that position, she had been doing that work for three years. So one of my predecessors must have hired her.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to the issue of the resupply convoys, both to the DutchBat peacekeepers and the civilian population in Srebrenica. You -- you mentioned that this was one of the areas about which you dealt with General Milovanovic. Would you please describe the procedure that you had to follow with respect to these reply convoys.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, one very unfortunate fact -- see, ordinarily at UN missions the UN troops have freedom of movement. In the beginning, that appears to have been the case in Bosnia as well. After some time, however, that was infringed upon, and that meant that we needed to request permission for displacement of convoys and we need to request permission from the party whose territory that was. So if we wanted to send a reply convoy to the enclave in Srebrenica, then we had to indicate a few days in advance how many vehicles we intended to send there, via which route, and with which load. And we had to request permission for that displacement. And ordinarily that would arrive very briefly in advance, and sometimes there would be restrictions or we wouldn't be allowed to send as many vehicles as we wanted to, or certain parts of the load were not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on each side - here speaking about the UNPROFOR side and the VRS side - how was the initial request for permission to resupply via convoy handled? At what level, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Once the needs had been established by the staff within a certain enclave, then the transport officer would determine how many vehicles were necessary to transport that load, and he would then ask -- and I think he did so by fax. He would complete a form requesting permission to be allowed to -- to move that convoy. And if everything went well and permission was granted, then I didn't need to get involved. If at a certain point permission was refused, then we would try it at a higher level, which was usually the level of the Chief of Staff, to see whether we could obtain permission after all, or we would inquire about the reason why certain things were being rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And with what frequency would you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My apologies. My microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With what frequency would you have convoys denied by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, but it happened very regularly that at the very least, requests were changed and requests were regularly refused, as well, and I won't say -- I wouldn't say that that happened every week, but it certainly happened every month. It depended on the period. At the beginning of my posting, it wasn't that common. But certainly in May and June that regularly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were dealing with General Milovanovic with respect to the denial of the convoys, how would you describe what you had to do in order to get permission from General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a lot of means at my disposal. I tried to use persuasive tactics to explain why these convoys were necessary, and then I would try to convince my counterpart, of the other party, that the permission had to be granted. Nine out of ten times that's what happened. Once I took it a step further. That was in early March 1995. And we threatened if the food convoy were refused, that the enclave would be supplied by air and, if necessary, violence would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "if necessary, violence would be used," what do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If they tried to block the supply flights by shooting at the aeroplane, then we would use our air weapons to fight our way in and to carry out those supply flights anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you said this was stated in March. At that time, did you in fact have any air resupply plan in place that would back up that threat, as you described it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Not yet at that time. That means that if we had had to execute it at that moment, we would have had to do an awful lot of improvising. But now that we were confronted with the fact that more and more convoys were being refused permission and the supplies were dwindling, we realized that we needed to draft a plan so that if a real emergency materialised, we would have to have a plan that we could execute to be able to supply our troops, if necessary, through violence. That was why General Smith assigned his staff to draft a plan for this eventuality, a very detailed plan. And I remember that we worked over two months on that, set everything forth in paper, and by the end of April the plan was ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not that plan was approved by -- length start with Mr. Akashi, for example. -- Let's start with Mr. Akashi, for example.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was a military plan. And, of course, it first had to be approved by General Janvier, but Mr. Akashi was aware of it as well and consented. And what I'd like to state for the record: This does not mean that the plan could automatically be carried out, because aeroplanes from different countries would be participating at the moment of execution. The permission would be required from all countries supplying troops here. So authorisation from all troop-contributing nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've described a -- a plan that required a lot of staff work and a lot of time. What were the conditions, General, between March, April, and May which justified devoting that amount of time and resources to an air-resupply plan so that you wouldn't have to follow the procedure that you were following already with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, the necessity of developing that plan arose from the increasing refusal to grant permission to resupply convoys, and thus resupplying the military people in the enclaves, as well as the civilians, became very difficult and the situation was deteriorating. And the plan was intended for the event that a situation became imminent where people were on the verge of starvation, and then we would provide supplies through -- if necessary, through violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from what you understood, sir, where was the decision actually made on the Serb side as to whether to approve or deny a convoy?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I assume the VRS headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to focus just for a moment on the fuel resupply. Do you recall off the top of your head how many fuel convoys were approved for DutchBat by the VRS between February and June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very clearly, because there weren't a lot of them. During my term, one convoy with fuel entered the enclave. That was the convoy in early March. And after that, all fuel convoys were rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the resupply convoys of food and other material, both for DutchBat and for the civilian population, did you receive any reports about what would happen to some of the convoys which would be approved en route to their destination?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll try to simplify it, if I -- if I might, sir. Did you ever receive reports, sir, that food and other material resupply convoys - not talking about fuel - would not reach the ultimate destination with its approved load?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Absolutely. That happened regularly as well. Even though permission was granted, somewhere along the route, at a control post or a check-point, vehicles were blocked, sent back. Sometimes the vehicle had to be unloaded but the convoy commanders were prohibited from doing so. So if a vehicle or a load was refused, then it would likely have to return mission unaccomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in -- in your time in Bosnia, sir, with respect to resupplying the eastern enclaves, which party, if any, was doing this blocking or sending-back the most?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, it was clear that that was the VRS, because you had to travel across VRS territory to reach the enclaves. Sometimes during the route preceding that, across Bosnian territory, but the -- the supplies were intended for Bosnians in the enclaves as well. So we didn't usually get problems there, but we did encounter problems with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So can you describe, sir, to what degree, in your experience, was UNPROFOR dependent upon the VRS to be able to resupply its peacekeepers in the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, entirely, because without permission from the VRS, we couldn't move those convoys and we were not in a position at the time to resort to violence, except by air. And that was a means that we wanted to -- it was extreme and we wanted to use that only in dire emergencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions on -- on this and one related topic, sir, before we move on. Did anything change during your six months concerning the DutchBat peacekeepers taking leave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems with that too. I would almost say, What did we not encounter problems with? But it did happen that the DutchBat soldiers left the enclave to go on leave, and a few weeks afterwards, when they tried to return, they would be blocked and would be refused permission to return to their base. The ultimate result was that the number of troops in the enclave had diminished from about 600 soldiers to about 350 soldiers. Clearly, after that we didn't authorise leaves any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who in the VRS -- with whom in the VRS did you deal about these leave problems?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, various levels were involved. Of course, as the Chief of Staff, I would start talking to my VRS counterpart about that. We also wrote official letters signed by General Smith, and the chief of the civil affairs division negotiated about this as well, all to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you yourself have contact with the DutchBat commanding officer about the resupply situation and the effects it had on DutchBat's ability to remain operational?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any formal direct contact with the DutchBat commander, because there was in fact a level in between. So strictly speaking, I had to interact via the headquarters in Tuzla with the DutchBat commander. On the other hand, because I was the senior Dutch officer, the highest ranking Dutch officer in the commando, I was empowered to contact my countrymen directly, and I could do that. I had a direct line. And obviously I did contact him regularly to ask how things stood and whether everything was well, especially when things were not well. I obviously contacted him more frequently to ask about the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did the DutchBat commander ever commit any of his complaints or concerns in writing to your command, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to give you a full answer. He did so both orally and in writing. At first, it was orally, to indicate which problems were being caused, for example, due to fuel shortages. So very quickly, the fuel shortages forced him to discontinue his motor patrols and he could only send out foot patrols. After a while, they also stopped using fuel to heat the buildings, to save the fuel, to keep the generators going that were needed to use the communication devices. And, of course, those are consequences that compromise operational usefulness. And when that -- when things became worse, I believe sometime in May, he drafted a first report about the situation. That was a written report presented through the official line of command, in which he explained how dismal his supply position was, both with respect to fuel, spare parts, munition, as well as the quality of munitions, the lack of food, and that this was -- this had seriously compromised his operational usefulness. I remember another report from early June in which he basically stated that he'd reached a point where operationally he was no longer able to do his job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we'll be turning to the VRS attack on the enclave in a few moments, General, but first, how would you describe the military situation, just generally, in terms of the activity around the Srebrenica enclave in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, the enclave was surrounded on all sides by VRS troops. We clearly had the impression that during the course of June the number of troops had been increased, and that raised questions about the intentions of the VRS, whether they intended to attack the enclave and what the purpose would be of such an attack; did they intend to seize part of the enclave, for example, the southern part across which there was an important supply route, or would they try to seize control of the entire enclave. That was a tough call. At first in our commando we believed that it would concern only the southern area. After a while, the VRS did indeed start attacking UN targets, and in June one of the observation posts was attacked and DutchBat was forced to leave those observation posts. In early July there was another step because successively more observation posts were being attacked and shot at, and those static posts at exposed sites, although they were protected by sandbags and barbed wire, they were certainly not -- they certainly couldn't withstand tank fire. So if they were fired on by tanks, the only thing to do was to abandon the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General, let me just back up for a quick moment. Just generally speaking, in terms of firing incidents or attacks by either of the warring parties in the month of June in the area of Srebrenica, do you recall receiving complaints by either of the warring parties about such attacks, firing incidents, and so forth? And if so, do you recall what you did about those complaints from either of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. There were complaints from both parties, both from the side of VRS and from BiH. The VRS complained about Muslim soldiers that would exfiltrate from the enclaves and that would attack villages on Serb territory. They complained that evidently the UN was unable to stop this. The BiH complained that they were being shot at by the VRS. The latter could also be observed by DutchBat. So we were well-positioned to check whether these complaints were justified. And actually, there was a third party in some cases; sometimes the UN itself was shot at. So protests about that were sent out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I just want to make sure of one thing; namely, that the interpretation is correct. The -- line 24 on the previous page, on page 18: "The BiH complained that they were being shot at by the VRS. The latter could also be observed by DutchBat." Did the witness say Dutch -- the BiH complained that they were being shot at by the VRS or bombarded by the -- by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure if the translation has been correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will clarify this. Both could be observed. Sometimes it was direct small-calibre fire, but since shots were often fired from the hills, we could see this. And in some cases, it was shelling, shooting with artillery or mortars; sometimes aimed at the positions of Muslim soldiers, sometimes also at random to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in response to these complaints from both of the warring parties, did you or anyone at your command issue any formal protests?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, of course, that would have to be something to be done by the DutchBat commander, to solve that and to put an end to these hostilities locally. But if the situation was under threat of getting out of hand or whether -- when it was impossible for them to gain control of the situation, of course he could ask his next higher in command to try at a higher level to put an end to these hostilities. And this happened a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And ultimately, do you recall protest letters being issued by either sector-level command or -- or BH-level command to both of the warring parties during the month of June?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This happened at some regular intervals, with the exception of using air support, writing protest letters was the only resource we had to try and do something about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the VRS attack on the enclave, and I want to ask you about several conversations you had with various high-ranking VRS officers during the course of that attack. First I want to turn your attention to the loss of a Dutch soldier, Private Raviv Rensen to Muslim fire on July 8th. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you briefly describe the circumstances of his death and what you did in response to his death.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. One of the observation posts was attacked, was fired at inter alia by a tank. After some time, the commander of the observation post decided that the situation had become untenable. He asked leave to abandon the observation post. That leave was granted. And the commander received the assignment to turn to the command at Potocari with his men. On the way back, they had to pass near BiH positions, who were totally in disagreement that this observation post was abandoned. They tried to stop the vehicle, unsuccessfully so. They also shot at the vehicle. And in the -- on that occasion, the board fire-man was hit and he died before reaching the compound. Naturally, the DutchBat commander reported this soon. Next I contacted the Sarajevo headquarters, the BiH headquarters, to protest against the situation there and to fiercely insist that they were to leave the DutchBat troops in the enclave unharmed and grant them freedom of movement. I also announced that this would be followed up by an official written protest. Naturally, I also protested with the VRS about the fact that they had attacked the observation post and about the fact that they were busy penetrating the enclave. I urgently insisted that they should withdraw their troops behind the treaty lines, truce lines that were -- had been agreed upon earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to be entirely clear, for the record, whose tank was this that was firing on the -- on the OP, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The OP was fired at by VRS troops, and the -- the vehicle that was on its way from the observation post of the compound, that was shot at by BiH troop -- troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And specifically the tank, who -- who did the tank belong to, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That belonged to the VRS. The Muslim troops in the enclave didn't have that heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did you personally make any contact with either of the warring parties in connection with this incident?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. As I just told you, I contacted the loss of the soldier with General Hajrulahovic. He was the person who was the Chief of Staff at the BiH headquarters in Sarajevo. And as far as the attack on the observation post was concerned, I had contacts with General Tolimir of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter number 2750 displayed on e-court, please. I'm not showing a English version yet. Is -- am I the only one or -- we're still waiting for it to be uploaded. Okay. I just wanted to be sure. And I have hard copies we can place on the ELMO and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems there --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- place before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems there may be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could move that just a little bit up or out and -- okay. Maybe a little bit higher so we can catch the -- the signature line. Perfect. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to -- to read this document?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This is a report of a telephone conversation that I conducted with the VRS headquarters. Particularly in that period when tension rose, we took the habit of drawing up reports of these telephone conversations. It would be drawn up by my MA with the aid of my female interpreter. These reports were mainly intended to inform internally other people within staff. To start with, the commander; then the head of civil affairs, and the head of the present information office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, sir, what was the name of your female interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The female interpreter was Svetlana. My MA was Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter. And his signature is underneath this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was it your practice at the time to actually review these reports after they were created?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Because it was I who had conducted the conversation, and I was responsible. I had to approve these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the accuracy of -- of this report, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In terms of content, it is 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you several more examples of these reports, General. And -- and to save time, was the same procedure and the same participants -- were the same procedure used and the same participants present - that is, yourself; your interpreter, Svetlana; and Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter - for all of these telephone conversations during this couple of days?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me say, my military assistant, Lieutenant-Colonel de Ruiter, and Svetlana were always present in these conversations. Svetlana obviously, because without her I was unable to conduct these conversations. My MA was functionally involved in all of these activities too. And in some cases, it could be that a fourth or fifth person was present in my office as well. But generally, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this conversation. It indicates that there were no generals available at the VRS headquarters, so you left a message, referring to a previous conversation with General Tolimir. Do you recall what the -- the content of your previous conversation with General Tolimir was? What was that about?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. The cause was the attack at the OP, the incident we just referred to, that afternoon at around 3.00 p.m. It was shelled and then had to be abandoned. And as I told you earlier, after having communicated my protests to the BiH troops, I subsequently contacted General Tolimir and protested against the attack on the observation post. Subsequently, insisting with him that this attack be stopped and that his troops be withdrawn behind the cease-fire lines. Since that hadn't materialised in the evening at about 7.30, I contacted him again in order to insist upon this once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this report notes that General Tolimir promised that UNPROFOR and UN positions would not be attacked. Subsequent to this conversation at 19.45, did General Tolimir keep his promise that UNPROFOR and UN positions would not be attacked?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The answer is short: No. As with all things we protested against in that period with regard to VRS attacks, they would always be denied -- they would always assure us forcefully that UN troops were not being attacked, which was absolutely at odds with the reports we received from DutchBat in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's move to the next day, July 9th, General. Did the VRS attack continue that day?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, more observation posts kept being attacked. Exactly how many were attacked on that Sunday, I don't remember that. Not off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if anything -- do you recall. Sorry. I was just pausing. Is it being interpreted properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I mean, while you're still speaking English, there's no point in asking, because we'll all hear yourself. It's only when the witness turns on to Dutch that -- that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll keep moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall, General, what, if anything, was being done with respect to repatriating Private Rensen's body?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This complicated my position. On the one hand, I had to protest vociferously about the events; and, on the other hand, I had to request assistance so that the body of the deceased soldier Rensen could be transported out of the enclave. I requested assistance, and quite honestly, I received such assistance. And that happened entirely as agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If -- if we may, let's look at 65 ter 2972, just for a moment. And, General, can you read that document on the right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I've already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention on the last paragraph. It indicates that "General Tolimir responded that he was not aware of his subordinate commanders obstructing the Casevac by road. He asked General Nicolai that his men go to Bratunac immediately, while he would order his troops to enable them to proceed to Zvornik. When on the BSA territory, his men would be received by his troops, he would immediately pass the instructions to the BSA units accordingly." Just a couple of questions on this paragraph, General. Do you know to whom General Tolimir was referring when he made this reference to "his subordinate commanders"?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as the last part, he meant -- he meant the local commander of the VRS on site, so in or around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just generally, what is General Tolimir talking about doing here?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If you would give me a moment -- just a moment to read the entire message, then I can refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, General.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember again. Aside from the fact that I spoke with General Tolimir about the return of DutchBat soldiers who had fled to Serbian territory from their OPs because they were afraid to move across the BiH positions, this was primarily about transporting the body of the soldier who was killed. I just said that it happened as agreed, but apparently there was one glitch. The first time they tried to transport the body across -- along the road to Bratunac, they were blocked by VRS troops. And I spoke with General Tolimir, asking him to instruct the people that we had agreed that the convoy was allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did General Tolimir take care of that glitch? And was the convoy allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That was resolved. And the remains of soldier Rensen were transported that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at 65 ter 2751, if we may. This particular document has a lot of text on it, General. If -- if it would be easier for you to have a hard copy, I -- I do have one available. Otherwise, please take your time and try to make out what you have there on -- on the screen. I know it's -- it's a lot of dense writing, but please take your time and -- and let me know when you've had a chance to -- to read the document.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it clearly on the screen. I'm finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall this conversation, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The situation kept deteriorating, and there had been extensive contact between the headquarters in Sarajevo and the headquarters in Zagreb about the situation that had materialised, and it became clear that only through letters of protest -- letters of protest alone would not resolved the matter. That was why I contacted General Tolimir again and urged him, once again, to withdraw his troops, as we would otherwise be forced to resort to other means of violence to force the troops to withdraw. And that in effect meant using air weapons. And I then spoke about having soldiers return -- allowing soldiers to return who had fled to Serbian territory. General Tolimir said that those soldiers had permission to return to their bases, but that proved incorrect. And General Tolimir asserted once again that the UN was not a VRS target and that they would not be shot at at all, and that conflicted with all reports issued by the DutchBat commander. And General Tolimir promised that he would check once again to ensure that his ground troops did not attack DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, if we look at the last paragraph on this document, it indicates, as you just said, that "General Tolimir promised he would check this information directly on the ground, although he said" -- or told you that he did not believe this was true. And he asked you to call him back in 30 minutes. Do you recall him doing that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did call back at some point, but not within 30 minutes. Later that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall trying to reach General Tolimir yourself after this phone call when you didn't hear from him in 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. At any rate, I tried. As far as I can remember, I tried a few times. But the documents available to you should tell you exactly when I succeeded, because I don't remember that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we have enough time before the -- the break to look at another, and that is 65 ter 2973. Actually, this is a rather long, General -- document, General. It's two pretty packed pages. So please take your time. We may not be able to finish it before the break, but take your time and read this, if you would.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The -- the prior telephone conversation you had was 9 July, 1750 hours. And now we're looking at a report of the same date, 1930 hours. What was the purpose of this call, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, then I would have to tell you what else happened that day within the UN network. After close consultation between the headquarters in Sarajevo and Zagreb and involvement on the part of General Janvier himself, it was decided that to send a clear message that the limit of what the UN would tolerate had been reached. So to this end, General Janvier instructed that parts of DutchBat blocking positions be taken - these are blocking positions in Dutch as well - south of Srebrenica. And, first of all, their purpose was to block the approaching Serbian troops; and, two, they were intended to create a situation so that if they tried to continue approaching Srebrenica, they would be in a situation where they had no choice but to attack the UN as well. And in that case, because both the civilian population was being threatened and the UN was being attacked, the entire international community would then understand that a situation had materialised that justified the use of air arms. And because we wanted to make this very clear to the Serbians, we drafted an ultimatum in writing to let them know that the consequences of their continuous attacks would be such, and this telephone call preceded that and it was, first of all, because I wanted to VRS to stop attacking the UN; and in addition to that, because they had already penetrated the enclave, so I urged that even if they desisted from their acts of violence, they had to withdraw their troops beyond the borders of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll have to leave it, I think, there, until we return from the break, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Thank you, General. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, General.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have the first page of 2973 again, please. And that would be on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The first paragraph, General, reports that you were curious about General Tolimir's information on the ongoing events in Srebrenica and you were concentrated on General Tolimir's confirmation of his previous message. Can you explain this passage just briefly, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that each time I told General Tolimir about what was happening - namely that, the UN was being attacked - he consistently denied it, and the last time before this phone call, he promised once again to inquire from his -- from the commander on site as to what was the matter. And each time again he continued to deny that UN troops were being attacked by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, where he tells you that he had passed the message on to his subordinate commanders and was informed that the VRS had no particular problems with UNPROFOR or the civil population in Srebrenica, how did that square with the information you were receiving at the time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: It was consistently incorrect. The DutchBat commander kept me continuously informed about what was happening. General Tolimir denied that in any way, shape, or form. And I'm fully convinced that he knew exactly what was going on, but he was unwilling to confirm that. And in the end, I told him, "Whether they're actually fighting or not at this point in time doesn't matter that much; the fact is that your troops have already penetrated the enclave more than four kilometres and they need to withdraw beyond the borders of the enclave."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just pick up on something you just mentioned in -- in that answer, sir. You described contacts that you had with Colonel Karremans. What were your sources of information during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, the most important source of information consisted of the situation reports that the DutchBat commander gave me either directly or via the intermediary of the headquarters of the Tuzla sector commander. In addition to that, we had some other information sources. There were English special forces in the enclave reporting directly to a special bureau at the Sarajevo headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, sir, what types of weapons were being used by the VRS during its attack? And do you recall approximately where they were located in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The entire enclave was surrounded by VRS positions, including various artillery positions and launching systems for multiple rocket launchers. There were mortar positions. The OPs were attacked in part by tanks. I certainly know that a T-55 was reported. That's a Russian hyper-tank. And there were shootings in several places with small-calibre arms and small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on the information you were receiving, how would you describe the VRS operation militarily, in terms of its organisation and -- and execution?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, at that point, it became crystal clear that the VRS was attacking the enclave. It was not immediately clear where they would stop, but they had penetrated far enough for them to have almost reached -- have reached the city of Srebrenica. So it was high time to stop the attack in its tracks and that's why we threatened to use air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll get to that in -- in a little while, sir. And just for the clarity of record, when you refer to the use of air power, you're referring to air-strikes or close air support, or both?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, at first close air support would be the most obvious. At that point, it was the only thing that the UN in Bosnia was empowered to use. Permission for air-strikes, so massive air attacks, that would have to be granted from New York. And the levels for that authorisation following the fiasco at the air attack in late May, that level had been raised. So at first we were talking about close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Returning back to the first page of 2973. And I'll actually slow down a little bit. I feel myself speeding up here. In the third paragraph of the English version - and this is also the third paragraph of the B/C/S version - you refer to a strong warning supported by the force commander, General Janvier, and Mr. Akashi that would be in writing. Was such a warning issued, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, on the evening of 9 July that warning was sent to the VRS headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll talk about that in a moment. Moving down -- and we'll have to, I think, go to the second page of the B/C/S, but it's at the very -- at the bottom of the English. General Tolimir repeated his report that there was no conflict between UNPROFOR, BSA, and the BiH civil population in Srebrenica." Again, based on what you knew at the time, was that a true statement or a false statement?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was incorrect. It was definitely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we move to the next page, General Tolimir tells you that the Bosnians were using six APCs either given by or taken from UNPROFOR. How did you respond to that information?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, somewhat irritated. It's unfortunate that you have to communicate that via an interpreter, because this accusation was so absurd that I was extremely irritated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, if we look at the second-to-the-last paragraph in the English - and we'll have to scroll down on the B/C/S to capture that - General Tolimir -- and it's the last sentence of that-second-to-last paragraph, promised to contact his subordinate commanders. Do you remember him promising to contact his subordinate commanders, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember everything that is stated here. But nothing happened. In fact, the opposite happened. Rather than the troops withdrawing, they continued their attack. So these promises that are not kept, that doesn't do us any good.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with this document. If we may look at 65 ter 2975, please. We'll just wait for the B/C/S translation. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, can you -- can you read the date and time-line and tell us what time this document reads and the date.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: 9 July, 22.20 hours, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as we can see, this is coming from the commander headquarters UNPROFOR, and the internal distribution. Who was the COS referred to there?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's the Chief of Staff of the headquarters, so that would be me, or that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this cover page indicates that "Attached is the final warning to the Bosnian Serbs. We've sent it as a CAPSAT to General Mladic and we will issue it as a press statement"? Do you remember that being done, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This document was drafted after an extended exchange of ideas between the headquarters in Zagreb and Sarajevo and was ultimately set forth in writing by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, who's General Smith's MA. And following its approval by both General Janvier and General Gobillard, it was sent to General Mladic -- or rather, to his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what this warning said in sum?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That's obvious, because the stage of the difficulties had advanced so far that this was our very last warning before we would resort to violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next page. The first line, General, reads: "The Bosnian Serb Army resumed attacks against the Srebrenica enclave on Friday, 7 July 1995, firing indiscriminately into the safe area and directly targeting UN facilities, causing several civilian deaths." Do you recall receiving information during this period of time that civilians had been killed by the VRS shelling or firing?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was reported on repeated occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Further on into that paragraph, it indicates that: "Two further UN OPs were overrun by the BSA that evening and 15 peacekeepers taken captive. A further 17 peacekeepers had been taken this afternoon." You indicated earlier in your testimony that some peacekeepers fled to the Serb side because they were afraid of passing through the Bosnian lines. Did you have any reports or information that some of the Dutch peacekeepers were -- were taken -- were taken more against their will than voluntarily from their OPs?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, their flight to Serbian territories, voluntary in the sense that they were still more afraid of passing the BiH positions. Of course, I -- it's no fun to surrender to one of the two parties, but they felt that the Serbians would treat them better than the BiH soldiers would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about with respect to other soldiers who had been manning other OPs which were overrun? Did you ever receive any information that they surrendered to the VRS under threat of arms, as opposed to fleeing towards them?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that happened as well, especially during the following days. So in some cases they surrendered; basically forced to volunteer. In other cases, they were threatened by arms and then they laid down their arms and surrendered to the Serbians. That happened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we -- if we look at the very bottom, the last paragraph, there's a reference to the blocking position and that the SRSG and the FC have decided that if the blocking position is attacked by VRS forces, NATO close air support will be employed. Is that what you had been describing just prior to the break, General, the blocking positions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you described numerous conversations that you had either directly or via the Sector North-East Command with Colonel Karremans. I'm not sure if we've actually said his name, but the commanding officer of the DutchBat Battalion in Srebrenica. Do you recall Colonel Karremans putting in written form his assessment and concerns concerning the VRS attack some time on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I definitely remember that. And what sticks most in my memory is his concern that air support would indeed be deployed. He feared that this would lead to massive retaliation, actions on the part of the VRS, and he said that unless the air forces were able to take out all VRS positions around the enclave in one fell swoop, he feared that there would be very serious retaliation by the VRS on his own troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you share that fear of massive retaliation by the VRS should close air support be employed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I certainly understood his point. The scenario was not strange to me because previously at the end of May, the VRS responded to air-strikes by shooting at enclaves. That was the most striking example, with the blood-bath in the centre of Tuzla. So it was extremely likely that that would be a possible reaction. As far as the UN leadership was concerned, that was no reason to forego this -- this air weapon, because we were certainly using -- we were certainly intending to deploy that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As opposed to employing. Is that correct, sir? At least for the time being.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: Despite the potentially serious consequences for DutchBat or the civilian population within the enclave, we certainly intended to use air weapons, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 2974 for a few moments, if we could. General, we're just waiting for the B/C/S translation. There we are. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That's the document in which Colonel Karremans expressed his concern about the situation that had arisen and the potential consequences that might materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we can see in the first paragraph references to shelling OPs, Srebrenica itself, and civilian casualties. You've already spoken about -- about those, so let's move to paragraph 2. He writes -- or he wrote: "During these three days, these operations have been executed by all means: Attacking ABiH and UN positions, shelling the enclave and suppressing DutchBat through intimidation by using artillery, mortars, and MLRS (M-63 and M-77)." What is MLRS, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: MLRS means "multi-launched rocket system," so a multiple rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans wrote that: "The BSA does exactly know what they are doing and till how far they can go. They do execute their operations according to a predominated and well-organised plan." Based on the information you were receiving, sir, was that consistent with what you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, this is an assumption. You can never prove it beyond any shadow of a doubt, but this did appear to be a carefully thought-out plan and we were increasingly getting that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the second page of this document. Paragraph 5 refers to an APC, a Dutch APC being lost to the VRS. Do you recall whether more than one APC was lost to the VRS during this operation, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, several fell into the hands of the VRS. At each observation post, there was one armoured personnel carrier, an APC. And if the crew surrendered, then the vehicle would also fall into VRS hands at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we move to paragraph 7, Colonel Karremans refers to several positions in the south-eastern part of the enclave being overtaken by the VRS and refers to the vicinity of the former observation post Echo. And then he states that he did express these concerns already last month. Can you just briefly expand on what he's talking about there, when he says, "I did express these concerns already last month." What's that about, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As I've stated previously during this session that the first observation posts fell into VRS hands in June, or at least had to be abandoned under VRS pressure. And that was the first warning that something was imminent. Karremans expressed his concern. He did not expect only one observation post to be involved; he expected follow-up actions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's just look at the last paragraph before we move on. He -- he writes that: "Using close air support in all possible ways is, in my opinion, not feasible yet. It will provoke the BSA in such way that both Srebrenica itself and OPs and compounds will be targeted by all means." Is this what you had referred to just a few moments ago in your testimony, General, this concern about having to take out all of the weapons systems in the event that close air support were employed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, this is the threat I was referring to recently. Karremans truly did fear that the VRS would deploy all of its means around the enclave as a retaliation for the use of air force and that the citizens of Srebrenica would be the victims of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the 10th of July. The blocking positions are in place. Briefly, General, what significant developments occurred that day?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In effect, the scenario proceeded as one of the possible ones that we had identified. The VRS troops continued their attacks and ultimately attacked the blocking position. And from that blocking position, the UN troops fired back. Because we had already identified this possible situation in advance, we had already completed preparations for requesting air support the day before. All the forms had been completed, and we merely needed to indicate the final update of the -- about the situation and sign off so that the procedure for requesting air support could happen very quickly. And we achieved that situation at the end of the afternoon of the 10th, and the result was that Colonel Karremans then requested air support. The request was sent to Sarajevo via the headquarter in Tuzla, and Sarajevo said, Yes, this is exactly the situation that we said would justify air support. And that meant that we immediately approved the request and sent it on to Zagreb, because Zagreb was the level for the ultimate approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, given what you've testified about in terms of the blocking positions and establishing the -- the preconditions for the authorisation of close air support, was this the first time that the conditions for close air support had in fact been met during the VRS attack, or had the conditions for employment of close air support been met on other occasions over the course of these couple of days?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Much earlier there were situations which would have justified the deployment of close air support, if you read UN Resolutions 824 and also UN Resolution 836. There it is clearly described under what circumstances the deployment of air support is justified, and certainly in the cases of self-defence by UN troops but also in cases where the civilian population in the protected areas were attacked. And it had happened already previously on several occasions. The reasons why no air support was used at that time is because at the end of May additional guide-lines or directives were issued for the deployment of air support and great restrictions were requested for in the deployment of air support, and that is why in the case of Mr. Karremans' request at 6 and 8 July for air support, no close air support was granted. And only after such a serious situation had developed as on the 10th of July, it was said, Well, if you don't do it now, it will never happen. And then it will be too late. And so at least at the level of Sarajevo headquarters, the permission was granted, but the level that was ultimately empowered to give that permission doubted for so long that ultimately they didn't grant that permission on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why not, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. The problem was that since they met about it for a long time, in the meantime it was becoming dark and there was also a situation in which the troops, both UN troops and VRS troops, had come to such close quarters that it would become difficult to distinguish one from the other, which made the actual deployment of air support a very risky business.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was close air support only and not the massive air-strikes that Colonel Karremans had talked about sought?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That is really the ultimate means that could have been used to do that. Permission would have been -- would have had to be asked for from New York, and that would have required even more time, and we would have never received that on time. So -- and also the second thought was that perhaps close air support alone would have been a more proportionate reaction and that that would have a sufficiently deterrent effect in order to make the Serbs decide to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you notify the warring parties of the fact that close air support had been approved on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As far as I know, in this case I warned both parties that air support had been requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may look very quickly at 65 ter 2976, please. Just take a moment -- take a moment, please, General, and read the document.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I have already read it. You just asked how I warned the parties. Well, this is the report of one of the relevant telephone conversations directed at the VRS headquarters in which I informed them that air support had been requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you something just a little bit different now, General. If we may have P02753 on e-court. General, this is a statement by General Gvero issued by the information service of the VRS's Main Staff on 10 July 1995. Do you recall reviewing this with me during your proofing session?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that the first time you'd seen this document, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may, let's move to the second page of the English. And I believe in the B/C/S it's going to be the third page. Because of the way the document was created, there are a couple of blank pages. So I think it's there. Perfect. Thank you. In the middle paragraph that begins with "They killed a United Nations soldier," General, there's a line in this statement by General Gvero that: "Our combat activities at the moment are directed towards simply neutralising the Muslim terrorists, and are in no way directed against civilians or members of UNPROFOR." When he says that "their combat activities are in no way directed against civilians or members of UNPROFOR," is that a true statement or a false statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This is absolutely incorrect. From earlier statements I have delivered today, it has become apparent that it was reported repeatedly that not only BiH positions were fired at but also at UN positions and at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We're done with that document. Let's move to the 11th of July. I don't think there's any dispute that the close air support was actually delivered that day. And we won't go into the details about how close air support was finally brought about. I think the Trial Chamber has already heard testimony about that. But quite simply, General, did the close air support stop the VRS attack?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The answer to that question is "no." There are various reasons for that. Firstly, the close air support was done at a small scale with a limited number of aeroplanes. Moreover, the use of close air support against highly distributed troops in a -- in a very hilly terrain is extremely difficult. I mean, in an open desert with -- against large-scale units, this air weapon is extremely effective. You can shell them. You can fire rockets at them. But in -- in this difficult terrain -- it's highly mountainous and a lot of vegetation. You have to find one single tank or just a couple of armoured combat vehicles while you fly over their heads at 100 -- or at 1.000 kilometres an hour, that is very difficult. Once you have tracked them, it's extremely difficult to actually fight them. So under those circumstances, it is not a very effective means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to focus on for -- for a little bit is what, if anything, the VRS said or did specifically as a result of the employment of the close air support.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we knew earlier each time the UN made use of air force, the VRS would respond vehemently against that. That was true this time as well. Concretely, it meant that in the afternoon of July the 11th we received a phone call from General Gvero at our headquarters with a message that -- summing things up, said that if we weren't going to stop immediately using air force, he would -- would have -- he would start -- he would have the compound at Potocari and surrounding areas shelled. Perhaps you remember the -- the pictures, but otherwise I could describe them. The compound at that point had been flooded by refugees from the city of Srebrenica. In the direct surroundings of the compound, there were thousands of refugees in the open air. So if shelling were to take place with artillery or mortars, this would develop into a tremendous blood-bath involving mainly innocent refugees. In addition, the vast majority of them were women and children. That threat was taken very seriously by us at the headquarters in Sarajevo. We should add to that that the situation at that point had already -- was that the -- the town of Srebrenica had already been occupied, so in our view, the battle had been fought. And at that point, running the risk of this kind of blood-bath prompted us into calling back the air force and to order them to stop their attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, were you the only person, other than the threat from General Gvero, were you the only person to receive a threat as a result of the employment of close air support?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent certain of this. I seem to remember that a warning was also issued to Colonel Karremans, a warning by the local Serbian commander to Colonel Karremans. But I'm not entirely certain about this, so I have to make some reservations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 2906, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. While we are doing that, when he refers -- when he -- when the gentleman refers to a warning by the local Serbian commander to Colonel Karremans, who would that be? Do you have an idea of who could that be, who you're referring to as -- as "local Serbian commander"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I wouldn't -- I would not know that. I do not know who the direct interlocutor of Colonel Karremans was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please take a moment and read it to yourself. And I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
